book.title: Sefer Luḳov : geheyliḳṭ der ḥorev-geṿorener ḳehile

overview.title: Jewish Łuków through Sefer Lukow
overview.summary: The memorial book presents Łuków as a Jewish community with documented religious institutions, schools, political movements, cultural life, families, and trades. Its testimony follows the community from centuries-old residence and rights through modern communal growth, German occupation, ghettos, deportations, murder, hiding, and resistance. Survivors then carried Łuków’s memory into new places through publications, memorial gatherings, and a pledge to remember the dead. Exploring these paths helps readers understand both the richness of the community that was destroyed and the testimony through which its history is preserved. [mention_60784a4a59ca237b5eed45e4; mention_c6ab49c2af6964c62ea9e416; mention_0d3f09ddd44dc8d2ca1f3563; mention_69efd85d788697ef4161ad94]

paths.title: How long had Jewish life existed in Łuków?
paths.description: This path traces the community’s documented legal, religious, and historical foundations, showing how Jewish residence in Łuków was connected to rights, institutions, and collective memory. By the end, readers will see that the community destroyed during the Holocaust had deep roots. [mention_60784a4a59ca237b5eed45e4; mention_938fd314b74841c6cd50a246]
paths.question: What foundations made Jewish communal life possible in Łuków?

steps.title: Residence and communal rights
steps.summary: The memorial book cites a Jewish rights charter issued on 10 May 1659, granting Jews rights of residence, commerce, crafts, property, a synagogue, and a cemetery. These rights provide the book’s evidence for an established community with both economic and communal institutions. [mention_60784a4a59ca237b5eed45e4; mention_938fd314b74841c6cd50a246]

steps.title: A long religious tradition
steps.summary: The book describes Łuków as a Hasidic town with several Hasidic groups and records the presence of rabbis and study houses. It also recalls the Great Synagogue, built at the beginning of the nineteenth century, showing how religious life was expressed through leadership, prayer, and study. steps.summary: The community-supported Talmud Torah taught hundreds of poor children, while a study house served older students and was supported by wealthy Jewish residents. paths.title: What did people do to make a living?
paths.description: This path reconstructs Łuków’s streets and economy through workshops, factories, shops, and family businesses named in the book. It shows a community sustained by both small household enterprises and larger employers. [mention_70051ea3dd119d301c5c3bc5; mention_90fe9d5e8d7c64e134e2ebc9; mention_3e853b47cd6ef70efe5473c0]
paths.question: How did work shape Jewish life in Łuków?

steps.title: A varied commercial world
steps.summary: The book names Jewish businesses selling cloth goods, stationery, oil and lighting supplies, and food, alongside bakeries, barbershops, and guesthouses. These accounts place Jewish work within the town’s streets and markets and reveal the everyday networks that connected households to customers and neighbors. [mention_2ae84b216f7b4980b684c299; mention_2f96e7facd1404efc0caa95b; mention_8563ee473dc1ad89cc18cc97; mention_df62100016d06b91f047107c; mention_9b311c4de3e29dbe323c3311; mention_a5ee180bb8ffdcbfb3755f24]

steps.title: Factories and skilled production
steps.summary: Jewish-owned production included a shoe factory, a soap factory, a spinning mill, an album factory, a brewery, and an oil press. Gastman’s shoe factory employed 300 workers, indicating that Jewish economic life included substantial industrial employment as well as small shops. steps.title: Economic change and movement
steps.summary: The book records the relocation of Gastman’s shoe factory from Warsaw to Łuków in 1906–1907 and the creation of a Loan and Savings Fund in 1908. It also records a 30-percent decline in Łuków’s Jewish population between 1914 and 1930, suggesting that opportunity and economic pressure both shaped mobility. [event_candidate_92892b8cbe0212f3dbd69616; event_candidate_d65f5cf47e91c1615c77991e; event_candidate_3df67ead2a8ae8ab80bb9a69]

steps.title: Mutual aid after war
steps.summary: Between 1918 and 1920, a public kitchen was established in Łuków with funds from American landsmen. The initiative shows how translocal Jewish ties supported people facing hardship in the town. [event_candidate_aafcd2b8406529e6ba668640]

paths.title: How did Łuków’s young people learn and create?
paths.description: This path follows competing and overlapping educational, literary, theatrical, and youth initiatives. Readers will understand Łuków as a place where Jewish culture was actively produced, debated, and passed to younger generations. [mention_ac3b9dd3075c9ee527d2d6ac; mention_6e4995243460b4f376933f77; mention_1c242248e1fe5259e8fb4e7c]
paths.question: What kinds of education and culture flourished before the destruction?

steps.title: Religious and girls’ education
steps.summary: Agudath Israel opened a Beit Yaakov school for girls, while the yeshiva continued to attract much of the youth. Together with the Talmud Torah and study houses, these institutions show several forms of religious education within the community. [mention_2960c7920839e9fab6e29c37; mention_6e3020982c02a9d09f1935f1; mention_5ffce3ac39b3494978ec1f44]

steps.summary: The secular Yiddish folk school formally opened in August 1928 and began classes on 1 September with one class. steps.title: Youth movements and shared activity

paths.title: How did Jews debate their future?
paths.description: This path examines elections, Bundist activity, Zionist initiatives, workers’ protest, and cultural associations. It shows Jewish Łuków as politically diverse and publicly engaged rather than socially uniform. [event_candidate_6ffae1afdfdb036f3c8dfced; event_candidate_4165359a2faeec590fb0eeb9; mention_39a1792553067c6f424781dd]
paths.question: Which political visions and civic activities shaped the community?

steps.title: Workers’ protest and repression
steps.summary: Workers demonstrated in Łuków in 1905, after which police dispersed the demonstration and made arrests. The book presents this episode as an early expression of Jewish workers’ political activity under pressure from authorities. [event_candidate_14c687ab13c38470aa278ad2; event_candidate_b19408745eb6a36b0d57d028]

steps.title: Bundist organization
steps.summary: The Bund was active in Łuków by 1904, organized early strikes, and formed a local organization in April 1916. Its later activity included political, professional, and cultural work, demonstrating that socialism operated through sustained communal organization. paths.title: How was the community destroyed?
paths.description: This path moves from German occupation and the ghetto to Aktionen, deportations, mass murder, and the emptying of camps. It teaches destruction as a process that affected institutions, families, and the town’s entire Jewish population. [mention_2fbbc3a812e820fe0f92dc02; mention_36b575815f63cbd20af2e6f6; mention_6d3b24c756c2709de866e2e5]
paths.question: What happened to Łuków’s Jews under German occupation?

steps.title: Occupation and confinement
steps.summary: The memorial book identifies the German occupation and describes a Jewish ghetto in Łuków, with a Judenrat located within the ghetto area. These accounts mark the transition from communal autonomy to imposed confinement and coercive administration. [mention_2fbbc3a812e820fe0f92dc02; mention_5936d51c1e8035704f34e05b; mention_c88998ebcbf13419c72c0bcb]

steps.title: Aktionen and deportations
steps.summary: The book recalls a first deportation addressed by the Łuków rabbi and announces an Aktion in Łuków in which Jews were killed or deported. On 16 July 1942, both camps were emptied and 1,050 people were transported, according to the cited account. [mention_513eb32363ba5fa214710ecd; mention_761eb66809a7e98e09124be9; mention_6d3b24c756c2709de866e2e5]

paths.title: How did people resist and survive?
paths.description: This path follows escapes from the ghetto, family hiding, aid, armed resistance, and partisan activity. It emphasizes the choices and dangers recorded in survivor testimony without treating survival as simple or guaranteed. [mention_0a944723421e2f4aca48adee; mention_4021de3502c30eddd847269a; mention_7cdb047c537a5caeb1344ae6]
paths.question: What forms did resistance and survival take?

steps.title: Escape into forests and hiding places
steps.summary: The book records Łuków Jews escaping into forests by using their knowledge of local paths, while the narrator’s family escaped to the forest after the Aktionen. Other accounts describe families hidden in a brickworks, a bunker, and a Polish person’s home. [mention_ced27f4379d6de3528849e36; mention_09673cc4ff5951a919f6fbd8; mention_9714bc962e4e276d3d4f89a2; mention_4021de3502c30eddd847269a]

steps.title: Aid and its dangers
steps.summary: The Domanski brothers are remembered for hiding Jews and being attacked by the Armia Krajowa, while the Kesselbrener family was hidden in Domina and later murdered. These testimonies reveal both the risks taken by helpers and the uncertainty surrounding rescue. [mention_75898d451626fd90768cd307; mention_cadccf2ba27b8bdf88169d74]

steps.title: Youth resistance in the ghetto
steps.summary: A youth resistance group formed and operated in the Łuków ghetto, and the book also describes resistance groups operating there. This matters because it places organized Jewish resistance within the ghetto itself, alongside escape and hiding. [mention_36b575815f63cbd20af2e6f6; mention_9fd1456627de07d942855a80]

steps.title: Fighters and underground networks
steps.summary: Reuven Heiblum is remembered as an organizer of underground activity in the Minsk ghetto who helped send medicine to partisans and later died in combat in 1943. Nahum Goldzak is remembered as a partisan who destroyed German supply columns, showing that some Łuków-born activists continued resistance beyond the town. paths.title: How did people preserve humanity under persecution?
paths.description: This path looks at testimony, family memory, song, theater, and practical acts of endurance during and after catastrophe. Readers will understand survival not only as physical escape but also as the preservation of relationships, culture, and meaning. [mention_050ee2f51724670e801883fb; mention_32b30d7e8b922d56a9139816; mention_de3d5080822d0679ae1c74bd]
paths.question: What did people carry with them through destruction?

steps.title: Family memory amid flight
steps.summary: One testimony recalls a four-year-old girl playing with her doll before departure, while another describes taking a mezuzah in a tallit bag. These details place children, homes, and religious objects inside the experience of forced movement and loss. [mention_1b4f9aca8b20716e828070d9; mention_1a7a73bc1736624ef3ca53c5]

steps.title: Theater and song in the camp
steps.summary: The camp dramatic circle performed Yiddish plays including Tuvia the Milkman and At Night in the Old Market. The Song of the Valley was sung as a camp anthem and symbol of hope, showing how performance and song sustained shared cultural expression. paths.title: Why was Sefer Lukow created?
paths.description: This path treats the memorial book as a survivor-produced act of remembrance, combining historical fragments, personal testimony, names, photographs, and commemorative gatherings. By the end, readers will understand both what the book preserves and why its perspective must be read as memorial testimony. [mention_0d3f09ddd44dc8d2ca1f3563; mention_3542383aca5513338de18de4; mention_ee0f0e7da1569da890ad106a]
paths.question: How did survivors remember a destroyed community?

steps.title: The book as testimony and warning
steps.summary: The Łuków Yizkor book is presented as testimony and as a warning to future generations, while Sefer Lukow documents Jewish life and the destruction of the community. Its purpose is therefore not only to list events but to keep the community present for readers who came after it. [mention_3542383aca5513338de18de4; mention_0d3f09ddd44dc8d2ca1f3563; mention_ee0f0e7da1569da890ad106a]
